stances.claim: The three 'granite-knuckled ladies' — Ombudsman Morales, Justice Secretary De Lima, and BIR Commissioner Henares — now have the legal duty to assess the evidence and determine whether to file criminal, forfeiture, and tax cases against Corona; the impeachment conviction removed his immunity and opened him to the full range of legal accountability.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-accountability activation: naming the three specific actors whose mandates now require prosecution consideration

stances.claim: The question of retirement benefits and honors for an impeached and convicted official is ultimately at the SC's discretion — given the precedent of Delsa Flores being stripped of all benefits for a far lesser SALN offense, the Court has both the power and the precedential basis to deny them to Corona.
stances.rhetorical_move: precedential-analogy argument: Delsa Flores's disproportionate penalty as the lower-bound precedent that makes Corona's denial legally plausible
stances.confidence: asserted as the SC's discretion to exercise

notable_anecdotes: The 'three granite-knuckled ladies' label — Ombudsman Morales, Justice Secretary De Lima, and BIR Commissioner Henares — as CJ's most memorable characterization of the post-conviction enforcement triumvirate, blending gendered admiration ('ladies') with toughness ('granite-knuckled') in a politically charged context.

Delsa Flores — a judiciary employee (not even a justice) stripped of all retirement benefits and accrued leaves merely for failing to disclose a market stall in her SALN — used as the disproportionate-but-precedential benchmark against which Corona's retirement benefits question must be assessed.

The unnamed justice whose retirement dinner was snubbed by 'most of his colleagues' after being fined P500,000 (the highest in judiciary history) for leaking a confidential internal document and then indefinitely suspended from the practice of law — a cautionary parallel that CJ inserts without naming, preserving decorum while establishing the precedent.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban systematically maps the legal consequences of the Senate's May 29, 2012 Judgment convicting CJ Renato Corona and imposing removal plus perpetual disqualification from all public office. Under the Constitution, the convicted party remains liable for prosecution -- criminally under RA 3019 (Anti-Graft Law), RA 6713 (Code of Conduct), and the Revised Penal Code; civilly for forfeiture of disproportionate assets under RA 1379 (though the one-year election bar prevents filing in court until after the May 13, 2013 senatorial elections); and administratively for disbarment. The impeachment trial evidence -- including the SALN waivers authorizing the Ombudsman to obtain bank documents -- is usable in subsequent proceedings with due process. BIR Commissioner Henares is also investigating possible tax violations using Corona's bank waiver. CJ identifies the three 'granite-knuckled ladies' -- Ombudsman Morales, Justice Secretary De Lima, and BIR Commissioner Henares -- as the institutional actors now duty-bound to assess the evidence and decide on filings. On retirement benefits (one month's salary per year of service, monetized leaves, five-year lump sum), CJ notes these are entirely within the SC's discretion, citing the precedent of Delsa Flores -- a judiciary employee stripped of all benefits merely for failing to disclose a market stall in her SALN -- as evidence that the Court has both the power and precedential basis to deny Corona retirement benefits and honors.
